query: For HfNbTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy, stress–strain behavior, thermal expansion, and elastic behavior at elevated temperatures remain insufficiently understood. What testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain these responses? Define a controlled comparison, the observations predicted relative to a baseline state, the temperature and response limits within which the hypothesis should hold, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In the HfNbTaTiZr refractory HEA, the unusual stress–strain behavior (including the yield strength plateau), moderate thermal expansion, and near temperature-independent elastic moduli at elevated temperatures (673–1073 K) are caused by a transition in the operative deformation mechanism. Specifically, as temperature increases, thermally‐activated screw dislocation slip becomes progressively replaced by edge dislocation motion (with accompanying dynamic recovery mechanisms such as thermal super‐jogging) that maintains a relatively constant dislocation glide resistance and effectively pins the lattice despite thermal expansion.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cold-rolled and subsequently annealed single-phase BCC HfNbTaTiZr, produced by standard casting followed by thermomechanical processing to ensure a homogeneous microstructure.
generation.intervention: Perform a controlled tensile or compressive mechanical test along with in situ high‐temperature dilatometry and neutron diffraction. Compare samples that are subjected to nanoindentation and bulk tests at various temperatures in the range 673 K to 1073 K. In parallel, characterize dislocation structures using TEM and/or HAADF-STEM to verify the dominant dislocation type.
generation.conditions: Specimens heated to and stabilized at temperatures between 673 K and 1073 K; strain rates on the order of 1 × 10^−3 s^−1 (or equivalent quasi-static rates) during mechanical testing; tests performed in inert atmosphere to minimize oxidation.
generation.structural_mediator: The evolution of the dislocation structure – specifically the dominance of edge dislocations (and evidence of dynamic recovery such as super-jogging) versus screw dislocations – which mediates the balance between thermal softening and work hardening, as well as the lattice response measured by elastic moduli and thermal expansion.
generation.mechanism: The mechanism is based on a temperature-induced slip mode transition where at lower temperatures screw dislocations control the yield behavior, but as temperature increases, edge dislocations (with higher activation barriers and super-jogging behavior) become dominant. This transition stabilizes the deformation resistance, limits thermal softening, and counteracts the effects of thermal expansion on the elastic moduli.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to a baseline measured at lower temperatures (or predicted by conventional thermally activated screw dislocation theory), the alloy will exhibit a plateau in yield strength and nearly constant elastic moduli over 673–1073 K, with a moderate increase in thermal expansion that does not degrade the mechanical performance. Microstructural observations should reveal an increasing fraction of edge dislocations and related recovery features with temperature.
generation.baseline: Mechanical properties (stress–strain curves, yield strength, elastic moduli) and thermal expansion measured at room temperature and lower elevated temperatures where screw dislocation motion is dominant.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold in the temperature range 673–1073 K under quasi-static loading conditions in specimens processed to a homogeneous single-phase BCC microstructure. Outside this range (e.g., at very low temperatures or above 1073 K where additional mechanisms or precipitation might occur), different behaviors may dominate.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative contribution of edge dislocation dynamics and thermal super-jogging to the overall plateau strength is uncertain, as are the potential effects of minor compositional inhomogeneities or incipient precipitation at the upper temperature limit.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare multiple batches of HfNbTaTiZr alloy with identical processing history. Conduct in situ high-temperature mechanical testing (tensile/compression tests) combined with dilatometry and neutron diffraction from 673 K up to 1073 K. Use TEM or high-resolution STEM to analyze the dislocation types at different temperatures. Compare the yield strength, elastic moduli, and thermal expansion trends with predicted plateau behavior. Simultaneously, perform strain-rate jump tests to see if the switching behavior correlates with the proposed edge dislocation activation.
measurements: Elastic moduli (via in situ neutron diffraction or resonant ultrasound spectroscopy)
Dislocation characterization (TEM/HAADF-STEM imaging to identify edge vs screw dislocations)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If, within the 673–1073 K temperature range, the yield strength does not exhibit a stable plateau or if microstructural analyses fail to show an increasing prevalence of edge dislocations (or signs of thermal super-jogging) compared to lower temperature samples, then the hypothesis that edge dislocation–mediated deformation is responsible for the observed mechanical and thermal behavior would be refuted.

cited_evidence.text: Overall, this comprehensive study provides evidence for the unique elastic and plastic deformation behavior of the single BCC solid-solution phase refractory HEA at elevated temperatures using in situ neutron experiments coupled with theoretical calculations. The results of the ND and characterization of the microstructure show the excellent BCC single-phase stability up to 900°C. Furthermore, the present alloy has the high yield strength and excellent plasticity at RT and softening resistance at elevated temperatures. The lattice strain evolution results show the distinctive elastic deformation behavior as an elastic isotropy at RT and less temperature dependency in the elastic anisotropic deformation behavior than conventional metallic materials at elevated temperatures. The single-crystal elastic moduli are obtained from the in situ ND data coupled with the Kroner model approach, showing excellent agreement with the experimental values determined from RUS measurements and first-principles calculations. AbstractNowadays refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are regarded as great candidates for the replacement of superalloys at high temperature. To design a RHEA, one must understand the pros and cons of every refractory element. However, the elemental effect on mechanical properties remains unclear. In this study, the subtraction method was applied on equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloys to discover the role of each element, and, thus, HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi were fabricated and analyzed. The microstructure and mechanical properties of each alloy at the as-cast state were examined. The solid solution phase formation rule and the solution strengthening effect are also discussed. Finally, the mechanism of how Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr affect the HfMoNbTaTiZr alloys was established after comparing the properties of these alloys.Keywords: high-entropy alloys, refractory high-entropy alloys, alloys design, elevated-temperature yield strength, solid solution strengthening effect
